concepts.title: Food Safety, Toxicity and Hazard
concepts.definition: Assurance that a food will not harm the eater when used as intended; toxicity names a substance's inbuilt power to injure, while hazard measures how likely injury becomes when the substance is misused or overdosed.
concepts.formula: qualitative trio -- safety is judged through toxicity plus hazard
concepts.key_idea: A toxic substance used correctly may pose little hazard; hazard grows with careless use.
question_patterns: define food safety, toxicity and hazard
how do toxicity and hazard differ from each other
why is assurance of safety tied to the intended use of a food
give one situation where a harmless substance becomes a hazard

solution_steps.action: define each of the three terms
solution_steps.explain: safety is the goal; toxicity and hazard are the two lenses for judging it
toxicity is a fixed property of the substance, hazard a probability tied to use

worked_examples.q: A substance's inbuilt power to injure is called what: toxicity or hazard?

concepts.title: Physical, Chemical and Biological Hazards
concepts.definition: Foreign matter that should never sit in food -- stones, hair, glass, nails, insect parts -- makes physical danger; pesticide residues, toxic metals and forbidden or excessive additives make chemical danger; and living invaders from worms and weevils down to bacteria, viruses, moulds and protozoa make biological danger.
concepts.formula: hazard classes -- physical plus chemical plus biological
concepts.key_idea: Biological hazards cause most food borne illness, and new pathogens keep appearing.
question_patterns: classify food hazards into physical, chemical and biological with examples
which objects count as physical hazards in food
name four chemical hazards that may enter food
distinguish visible from invisible biological hazards
why are biological hazards the leading cause of food borne illness

solution_steps.action: sort examples into the three classes
solution_steps.explain: stones and hair; pesticides and dyes; worms, bacteria and viruses
physical hazards are visible, chemical and microbial ones need testing

worked_examples.q: Stones, hair and glass in food make which hazard: physical or chemical?

concepts.title: Food Infection versus Food Intoxication
concepts.definition: Infection occurs when live germs swallowed with the food set up house in the body and multiply, as Salmonella from raw milk, eggs or cross contaminated boards does; intoxication occurs when a toxin already brewed in the food acts, even after the microbe that made it is dead, as with Staphylococcus aureus carried on skin and in throats.
concepts.formula: two routes -- live organisms multiply inside, or preformed toxins act directly
concepts.key_idea: Toxins carry no smell, taste or look, so good appearing food can still poison; about half of healthy people carry Staphylococcus.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe105.txt, food infection and intoxication (approx lines 216-241)
question_patterns: distinguish between food infection and food intoxication
how does Salmonella reach food through cross contamination in a kitchen
why can a food that smells and looks fine still cause intoxication
which organism commonly carries toxin into food from the handler's own body
what are the symptoms of a Salmonella infection
why does inadequate cooking let Salmonella survive

solution_steps.explain: swallowed live cells multiply in the gut; preformed poisons strike regardless of cell death
Salmonella for infection with diarrhoea, fever and cramps; Staphylococcus aureus for toxin mediated illness

worked_examples.q: Which illness route involves live germs multiplying inside the body: infection or intoxication?

concepts.title: Contamination and Adulteration
concepts.definition: Contamination is the arrival of objectionable matter -- chemicals, microbes, dilutants -- at any stage from field to table, while adulteration drags quality down by mixing in inferior material or by drawing out the valuable part of the food.
concepts.formula: quality loss -- contamination incidental, adulteration adds inferior or removes valuable
concepts.key_idea: Adulterants are the specific substances that make a product unsafe to eat.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe105.txt, contamination and adulteration definitions (approx lines 267-281)
question_patterns: define contamination and adulteration
how does adulteration lower the quality of a food product
what are adulterants
give one example each of contamination and adulteration
which stages of the food chain allow contamination to occur

solution_steps.explain: contamination may be accidental at any stage; adulteration implies lowered value through substitution or extraction
foreign matter for one, inferior substitutes or removed components for the other

worked_examples.q: Mixing inferior material into food to drag quality down is called what?

concepts.title: Food Quality and Its Attributes
concepts.definition: Food quality collects every attribute that shapes a buyer's judgement: the negatives -- spoilage, contamination, hazards -- and the positives -- colour, flavour, texture, appearance, nourishment -- with safety as the entry ticket to quality at all.
concepts.formula: quality = negative attributes plus positive attributes, safety first
concepts.key_idea: Sensory traits, nutrition and social concerns merge into one holistic verdict on a product.
question_patterns: what is meant by food quality
name the positive and negative attributes that shape food quality
why is safety called a precursor of quality
which sensory properties enter a judgement of quality
how do storage changes in appearance and odour signal falling quality

solution_steps.action: split attributes into positive and negative sets
solution_steps.explain: colour, flavour, texture versus spoilage, adulteration, hazards
no sensory excellence can rescue an unsafe product

worked_examples.q: Which attribute is the entry ticket to food quality: safety or sweetness?

concepts.title: Levels of Food Standards and Voluntary Marks
concepts.definition: Standards run on four coordinated planes -- a company's in house rules, national rules from FSSAI, regional group legislation and international codes from ISO and Codex -- while voluntary certification such as the ISI mark of BIS and Agmark grades farm products for the buyer.
concepts.formula: standards ladder -- company to national to regional to international
concepts.key_idea: Agmark covers agricultural raw and processed goods; the ISI mark certifies processed foods under BIS.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe105.txt, Food Standards and voluntary certification (approx lines 331-365)
question_patterns: list the four levels at which food standards operate
which national body issues India's food standards
differentiate between the ISI mark and Agmark
what is voluntary product certification
name the organisations that publish international standards

solution_steps.action: stack the four planes in order
solution_steps.explain: company copies usually mirror national rules; regional and international codes harmonise trade
BIS ISI mark for processed foods, Agmark for agricultural produce

worked_examples.q: Which mark grades agricultural products: Agmark or ISI?

concepts.title: FSSA 2006 and the FSSAI
concepts.definition: The Food Safety and Standards Act of 2006 gathered India's scattered food laws into one statute and created FSSAI, the authority that frames science based standards and regulates manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import of food.
concepts.formula: one act plus one authority consolidate all food law
concepts.key_idea: The Act shifted Indian law from compositional vertical standards to horizontal safety standards and data collection, alerts and training.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe105.txt, FSSA 2006 and FSSAI functions (approx lines 368-441)
question_patterns: what is the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 meant to do
list the functions mandated to FSSAI
how does the 2006 Act differ from the earlier PFA approach
which older orders were consolidated under the Act
how does FSSAI support state governments on food policy
what role does FSSAI play in spreading awareness about food safety

solution_steps.explain: PFA 1954 and the fruit, meat and vegetable oil orders merged into one umbrella
standards, accreditation of labs, scientific advice, surveillance data, consumer information, training

worked_examples.q: Which act gathered India's food laws into one statute in 2006: the FSSA or the PCA?

concepts.title: Codex, ISO and the WTO
concepts.definition: Codex Alimentarius is the intergovernmental food code that nations adapt into their own rules, ISO publishes voluntary quality management references such as ISO 9000, and the WTO, born in 1995, keeps trade in goods, services and ideas flowing fairly and predictably.
concepts.formula: three pillars -- Codex standards plus ISO management plus WTO trade rules
concepts.key_idea: Codex moves slowly and sets minimums; ISO describes current best industrial practice and refreshes every five years.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe105.txt, Codex, ISO and WTO sections plus comparison box (approx lines 397-514)
question_patterns: what is Codex Alimentarius and why is it important
how do Codex and ISO standards differ
what is ISO 9000 concerned with
when was the WTO established and what is its main objective
through which ministry does India participate in Codex
why must every trading country protect food safety under the WTO agreement

solution_steps.action: define each body and its output
solution_steps.explain: food code, management standards, trade administration

solution_steps.action: contrast Codex with ISO using the comparison box
solution_steps.explain: minimum acceptable versus current industrial practice; slow change versus five yearly review

worked_examples.q: Which intergovernmental food code do nations adapt into their own rules: Codex Alimentarius or ISO 9000?

concepts.title: Food Control: Inspection and Analysis
concepts.definition: A working control system rests on two legs: appointed inspectors who verify that food is produced, stored and distributed to rule, and accredited laboratories with trained analysts who can chase contaminants, biotoxins, pathogens and viruses in the samples.
concepts.formula: control system = food inspection plus analytical capability
concepts.key_idea: Without state of the art labs and skilled analysts, standards remain paper promises.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe105.txt, Food Inspection and Analytical capability (approx lines 515-529)
question_patterns: what are the two parts of an effective food control system
who appoints food inspectors and what do they verify
why do laboratories need accreditation
list the contaminants a good food laboratory must be able to detect
how does inspection confirm conformity to standards

solution_steps.explain: field inspection and laboratory analysis
environmental chemicals, biotoxins, pathogenic bacteria, viruses, parasites

worked_examples.q: Food control rests on inspection plus accredited what: laboratories or kitchens?

concepts.title: Safety Management Systems: GMP, GHP and HACCP
concepts.definition: GMP makes manufacturers act before problems arise, GHP stretches hygiene from farm to shop, and HACCP examines every raw material and every process step for its power to breed hazards, fixing control measures at the exact stage where trouble can start.
concepts.formula: three systems -- GMP plus GHP plus HACCP covering the whole chain
concepts.key_idea: HACCP beats end product testing because it catches hazards where they occur instead of after the batch is made.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe105.txt, management systems and Why implement HACCP (approx lines 530-605)
question_patterns: explain GMP, GHP and HACCP as food safety management systems
why is HACCP called a preventive approach
how does HACCP differ from end product inspection and testing
list the stages of the food chain that HACCP evaluates
why did the FSSA place responsibility for safe food on producers through HACCP
what benefits does HACCP bring to exporters and distributors

solution_steps.explain: proactive manufacture, farm to store hygiene, stage wise hazard analysis
cheaper, faster and safer than testing only the finished product; FSSA 2006 leans on it

worked_examples.q: Which system fixes controls at the exact stage where hazards can start: HACCP or end-product testing?

concepts.title: Careers in Food Safety and Quality
concepts.definition: Quality control labs, public and private testing agencies, certification bodies and HACCP teams hire analysts, inspectors, auditors and managers, while self employment opens through analytical laboratories, safety consultancy and sanitation education.
concepts.formula: career map -- analysts plus inspectors plus auditors plus HACCP specialists plus consultants
concepts.key_idea: The sector needs expertise in food chemistry, processing, analysis, microbiology, laws and sensory evaluation, and accounts for about 26 per cent of GDP.
concepts.textbook_ref: lehe105.txt, Scope and Career Avenues (approx lines 606-673)
question_patterns: list the career avenues in food safety and quality
which jobs can a food safety professional hold in regulatory agencies
what self employment options exist in this field
which subjects must a food safety professional master
name the roles a food industry quality control unit offers
what does an internal food auditor do

solution_steps.explain: regulators, industry labs, certification agencies, academia and voluntary bodies
chemistry, processing, analysis, microbiology, food laws, sensory science

worked_examples.q: Food safety careers demand chemistry, analysis, microbiology, laws and which evaluation of taste: sensory or financial?

concepts.title: Bacterial Doubling Time
concepts.definition: A bacterium that doubles on a fixed clock grows by powers of two; dividing the elapsed minutes by the doubling time gives the number of doublings, and the starting count times two raised to that power gives the final load.
concepts.key_idea: Salmonella doubles every 20 minutes, so two hours of neglect multiplies a small load sixty four fold.
question_patterns: Salmonella doubles every 20 minutes; if 500 cells sit on a salad for 2 hours, how many cells are present
calculate the bacterial count after a stated time when the starting load and the doubling time are given
a broth starts with 125 organisms that double every 20 minutes; find the load after 1 hour
how many doublings occur in 3 hours for a microbe with a 20 minute doubling time
work out the final population of bacteria from the initial count and the elapsed time

solution_steps.explain: divide elapsed minutes by the doubling time

solution_steps.action: raise two to that power and scale the start
solution_steps.explain: each doubling multiplies the load by two

worked_examples.q: Salmonella doubles every how many minutes: 20 or 200?

concepts.title: Adulterant Percentage Tests
concepts.definition: The tea stalk and pepper light berry tests weigh the unwanted fraction against the whole sample and report it as a percentage, which is then judged against the permitted ceiling.
concepts.key_idea: Stalks in tea should stay under 25 per cent; a high light berry share in pepper signals extraction of the good berries.
question_patterns: a 5 gram tea sample leaves 1 gram of dried stalks; calculate the percentage of stalks and compare with the 25 percent limit
10 grams of pepper yields 2 grams of floating light berries; find the percentage of light berries
how is the percentage of stalks in tea computed from the weighed fractions
compute the adulterant percentage when the separated portion and the original sample weights are stated
a tea lot shows 3 grams of stalks from a 20 gram sample; does it respect the permitted ceiling

solution_steps.action: divide the separated portion by the sample weight
solution_steps.explain: the quotient compares the unwanted part with the whole

solution_steps.action: scale the ratio to a percentage
solution_steps.explain: multiply by one hundred to express as per cent

worked_examples.q: Tea stalks should stay under what percent: 25 or 2.5?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A contaminated salad carries {starting_count} Salmonella cells and stands at room temperature for {elapsed_minutes} minutes. With a doubling time of {doubling_minutes} minutes, how many cells are present then?

solution_template.explain: 500 x 2 to the sixth = 500 x 64 = 32000 cells

worked_examples.question_pattern: A {sample_weight} gram tea sample yields {part_weight} grams of dried stalks after boiling and drying. Find the stalk percentage and state whether it stays inside the 25 per cent ceiling.

solution_template.explain: 0.2 x 100 = 20 per cent, inside the 25 per cent limit

worked_examples.question_pattern: Sort these hazards into physical, chemical and biological: hair, pesticide residue, tapeworm, stone, metanil yellow, mould.

solution_template.explain: hair and stone are physical; pesticide residue and metanil yellow are chemical; tapeworm and mould are biological
physical hazards are visible; chemical and biological ones usually need tests
